message.content:
You are reverse-engineering the Python library `furl` purely as a BLACK BOX by running a precompiled executable. You may NOT read furl's source. You may NOT run `python` (it is not available). Work only from observed behavior.

The executable is: /workspace/dataset/test2_executable
It is exactly equivalent to this Python program:

    import argparse
    from furl import furl
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.set(host=args.b).url)

So: --a is an arbitrary URL string parsed by furl(); --b is a host string assigned via .set(host=...); stdout is the resulting .url followed by a newline.

GOAL: produce an implementation-grade spec so that someone can reimplement this from scratch in pure JavaScript with byte-identical stdout.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT
- Run it directly, e.g.: /workspace/dataset/test2_executable --a 'http://x.com/p' --b 'n.com'
- It is a PyInstaller binary; each run takes ~0.2-0.5s. Batch many cases per bash call, but keep each bash call to <= ~100 cases so you do not hit the 120s tool timeout. Prefix each run with `timeout 20`.
- ALWAYS use this robust batching pattern (real TAB characters between the two fields):

    cd /workspace/dataset
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r A B; do
      printf '%s\t%s\t=> ' "$A" "$B"
      timeout 20 ./test2_executable --a "$A" --b "$B" 2>&1 | head -1
    done <<'EOF'
    http://x.com/p	n.com
    /rel/path	n.com
    EOF

  The quoted heredoc delimiter <<'EOF' prevents any shell expansion, so you can put backslashes, dollar signs, quotes and backticks in the data safely.
- On success stdout has the URL and exit code 0. On failure stdout is EMPTY, a Python traceback goes to stderr, and exit code is 1. Redirect deliberately (2>/dev/null vs 2>&1) and check `echo $?` when the distinction matters.
- When whitespace or invisible characters matter, pipe stdout through `od -c`.
- To isolate --a parsing, hold --b fixed at a boring valid host like `n.com`. To isolate --b behavior, hold --a fixed at `http://a.com/p`.
- IMPORTANT: because the host is always overwritten by --b, the original host text in --a only matters for (a) where the authority/netloc ends and the path begins, (b) whether an authority existed at all, (c) the port, (d) the userinfo. Do not waste runs on original-host spellings unless testing delimiting.
- Useful already-established baseline facts (verify, do not blindly trust):
  * scheme and host are lowercased; path/query/fragment case is preserved.
  * The final assembly behaves like Python's urllib.parse.urlunsplit((scheme, netloc, path, query, fragment)): if netloc is truthy, OR (scheme is truthy AND scheme is in urllib's uses_netloc list AND path does not start with '//'), then a '/' is prepended to a non-empty path that does not start with '/', and '//'+netloc is prefixed; then 'scheme:' is prefixed if scheme; then '?'+query if query is truthy; then '#'+fragment if fragment is truthy.
  * Default ports are elided: http://h:80/ -> http://h/ , https://h:443/ -> https://h/ , ftp://h:21/ -> ftp://h/ .
  * Query values are decoded then re-encoded: '?a=1%202' -> '?a=1+2' ; '?a=1;b=2' -> '?a=1%3Bb%3D2' ; '?a=ü' -> '?a=%C3%BC'.
  * Path segments are decoded then re-encoded: '/a b/c' -> '/a%20b/c' ; '/a%20b' stays '/a%20b' ; '/../a/./b' is NOT normalized.
  * --b non-ASCII is IDNA/punycode encoded: 'ünïcode.com' -> 'xn--ncode-cta3g.com'.
  * --b that is invalid raises: ValueError: Invalid host '<b>'. Host strings must have at least one non-period character, can't contain any of '!@#$%^&'"*()+=:;/', and can't have adjacent periods.
  * --b = '' does NOT raise; 'http://a.com/p?x=1#f' + '' -> 'http:///p?x=1#f'.

DELIVERABLES (all three are required)
1. Write a thorough, exhaustive spec to /workspace/specs/NAME.md (substitute your dimension NAME below). Every rule you established, each with the concrete evidence (input -> output) that proves it. Include tables. Explicitly flag anything you could NOT determine. This file is the implementation spec.
2. Append EVERY case you ran to /workspace/specs/cases/NAME.b64 — one case per line, format `<base64 of the --a value>\t<base64 of the --b value>` (TAB separated). Use this helper so it is exact:

    emit(){ printf '%s\t%s\n' "$(printf '%s' "$1" | base64 -w0)" "$(printf '%s' "$2" | base64 -w0)" >> /workspace/specs/cases/NAME.b64; }

   Include boring cases too — this becomes a differential-test corpus. Aim for at least 120 cases. Do not include the expected output (a separate harness regenerates it).
3. Return your structured findings.

CONSTRAINTS
- Do NOT write anything to /output. Do NOT create or modify any .mjs/.js files. You are a prober only.
- Do not use jq (unavailable). Standard coreutils, bash, base64, od are available.

YOUR ASSIGNED DIMENSION:
NAME = default-ports. Build the DEFINITIVE default-port table furl uses to decide when to elide a port from the output, and nail down all port parsing/validation edge cases.

Method: for scheme S and candidate default port P, run --a 'S://a.com:P/p' --b 'n.com'. If output is 'S://n.com/p' the port was elided (P is S's default); if 'S://n.com:P/p' it was kept. Probe at least these schemes against their plausible IANA defaults, and also cross-check each scheme against a WRONG port to confirm the port is otherwise preserved: http 80, https 443, ftp 21, ftps 990, sftp 22, ssh 22, telnet 23, smtp 25, smtps 465, submission 587, imap 143, imaps 993, pop 110, pop3 110, pop3s 995, nntp 119, nntps 563, news 119, snews 563, ldap 389, ldaps 636, gopher 70, wais 210, dns 53, tftp 69, irc 194, ircs 6697, rsync 873, svn 3690, git 9418, ws 80, wss 443, rtsp 554, rtsps 322, rtspu 554, mms 1755, nfs 2049, prospero 1525, shttp 80, file (none), mailto (none), and an unknown scheme 'zzz' with port 80. Report the exact mapping, and note any scheme where a port is NEVER elided.

Also determine, holding --b 'n.com':
- Port with no scheme: '//a.com:80/p' and '//a.com:8080/p' — is 80 elided when there is no scheme?
- Empty port: 'http://a.com:/p' — kept, dropped, or error?
- Port 0: 'http://a.com:0/p'. Leading zeros: 'http://a.com:080/p', ':0080'. Very large: ':65535', ':65536', ':99999', ':4294967296'.
- Non-numeric port: 'http://a.com:abc/p', ':8a', ':-1', ':+80', ':8.0', ':0x50', ': 80', ':80 '. Which raise ValueError and with WHAT exact message? Capture the exact final stderr line and the exit code for each.
- Does the port survive when --b changes the host? Does --b ever affect the port (e.g. --b '' with a port)?
- Uppercase scheme with default port: 'HTTP://a.com:80/p'.
- Does an IPv6 host with a default port elide it: 'http://[::1]:80/p'?

Black-box derived from `/workspace/dataset/test2_executable`
(`furl(--a).set(host=--b).url`). Every rule below has at least one observed
input -> output witness. Case corpus: `/workspace/specs/cases/default-ports.b64`
(506 cases).

---

## 1. Model of where the port comes from and goes

Parsing (`furl(--a)`) produces a `port` that is either `None` or an `int` in
`1..65535`. Rendering (`.url`) emits `:<port>` after the host **iff** the port
is set **and** it is not the default port for the (lowercased) scheme.

Pseudocode of the whole port lifecycle:

```
# --- parse time, inside furl(a) ---
authority = <netloc substring of --a>            # see §7 for when this exists
userinfo, hostport = rsplit(authority, '@', 1)   # '@' optional
if hostport starts with '[' and contains ']':
    host   = up to and including ']'
    rest   = after ']'
    portstr = rest[1:] if rest startswith ':' else None
else:
    if ':' in hostport:  host, portstr = rsplit(hostport, ':', 1)   # LAST colon
    else:                host, portstr = hostport, None

if portstr is not None:                # NOTE: '' counts as "not None"
    if not isDigitPy(portstr):                       # Unicode-aware, see §5
        raise ValueError("Invalid port '" + portstr + "'.")
    n = intPy(portstr)                               # may itself raise, see §5
    if not (0 < n <= 65535):
        raise ValueError("Invalid port '" + portstr + "'.")
    port = n
else:
    port = None
# host is validated only AFTER the port (see §6)

# --- render time, inside .url ---
scheme_lc = lower(scheme)  if scheme is not None else None
if port is not None and port != DEFAULT_PORTS.get(scheme_lc):
    netloc_out = host_out + ':' + decimalString(port)
else:
    netloc_out = host_out
```

  * `http://a.com!:8080/p` -> `Invalid host 'a.com!'. ...`
  * `http://a.com::abc/p` -> `Invalid port 'abc'.` (host would be `a.com:`)
  * `http://a.com::80/p` -> `Invalid host 'a.com:'. ...` (port `80` is fine)
  * `http://a.com:80:90/p` -> `Invalid host 'a.com:80'. ...` (port `90` fine)

The last two also prove the host/port split is `rsplit(':', 1)` — the **last**
colon wins.

---

## 7. When there is no port at all

### 7a. Port-looking text outside the authority is not a port

| `--a` | output |
|---|---|
| `http://a.com/p:80` | `http://n.com/p:80` |
| `http://a.com/:80` | `http://n.com/:80` |
| `http:///p:80` | `http://n.com/p:80` |
| `http://a.com?p=:80` | `http://n.com?p=%3A80` |
| `http://a.com#:80` | `http://n.com#:80` |
| `http:a.com:80/p` | `http://n.com/a.com:80/p` |
| `http:/a.com:80/p` | `http://n.com/a.com:80/p` |
| `http:80/p` | `http://n.com/80/p` |
| `ws:a.com:80/p` | `ws://n.com/a.com:80/p` |
| `mailto:a@b.com:80` | `mailto://n.com/a@b.com:80` |
| `a.com:80/p` | `a.com://n.com/80/p` (`a.com` parsed as the scheme!) |

### 7b. TAB / CR / LF are removed from everything after the scheme

Consistent with CPython's `urlsplit` deleting `\t`, `\r`, `\n`. **But the
scheme furl reports keeps them**, which changes the default-port lookup.

| `--a` | output | note |
|---|---|---|
| `http://a.com:<TAB>80/p` | `http://n.com/p` | tab removed, port==80, elided |
| `http://a.com:80<TAB>/p` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com:8<TAB>080/p` | `http://n.com:8080/p` | |
| `http://a.com:<LF>80/p` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com:80<LF>/p` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com:8<CR>0/p` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com<TAB>:80/p` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com:80/p<CR>` | `http://n.com/p` | |
| `http://a.com:80/p<TAB>q` | `http://n.com/pq` | removed from path too |
| `http<TAB>://a.com:8080/p` | `http<TAB>://n.com:8080/p` | tab **kept** in scheme |
| `http<TAB>://a.com:80/p` | `http<TAB>://n.com:80/p` | scheme != `http`, so 80 is **kept** |
| `ht<TAB>tp://a.com:8080/p` | `ht<TAB>tp://n.com:8080/p` | |

Non-`\t\r\n` invisible characters are **not** removed: NBSP (` `) and
ZWSP (`​`) inside a port produce the 5a error, and `` at the front
of a URL is percent-encoded into the path (`%7F...`).

### 7c. A URL whose first character is C0/space loses the whole authority — including the port

If `--a[0]` is in `�`-` ` (space, TAB, LF, CR, VT, FF, ``,
``, ...), furl ends up with **no scheme, no userinfo, no host and no
port**; only path/query/fragment survive. Crucially **no port validation runs**,
so even an invalid port is silently discarded.

| `--a` (`--b n.com`) | output |
|---|---|
| `' http://a.com:80/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' http://a.com/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' zzz://a.com:80/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'   http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'<TAB>http://a.com:80/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'<CR>http://a.com:80/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'<VT>http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'<FF>http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `'http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' http://u:pw@a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` (userinfo gone too) |
| `' http://a.com:8080/x/y'` | `//n.com/x/y` |
| `' http://a.com:8080'` | `//n.com` |
| `' http://a.com:8080/p?q=1#f'` | `//n.com/p?q=1#f` |
| `' //a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' /p'` | `//n.com/p` |
| `' xxx'` | `//n.com/xxx` |
| `' http://a.com:0/p'` | `//n.com/p` — **rc=0, NO error** |
| `' http://a.com:abc/p'` | `//n.com/p` — **rc=0, NO error** |
| `' http://a.com:65536/p'` | `//n.com/p` — **rc=0, NO error** |
| `' http://a.com!:8080/p'` | `//n.com/p` — **rc=0, NO error** |
| `' http://a.com::/p'` | `//n.com/p` — **rc=0, NO error** |

Contrast with a leading char that is **not** C0/space, where the whole string
becomes the path (and the port likewise never exists, but the text survives):

| `--a` | output |
|---|---|
| `1http://a.com:80/p` | `//n.com/1http://a.com:80/p` |
| `+http://a.com:80/p` | `//n.com/+http://a.com:80/p` |
| `'http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/%7Fhttp://a.com:8080/p` |
| `' http://a.com:8080/p'` | `//n.com/%C2%A0http://a.com:8080/p` |
| `'X http://a.com:8080/p'` | `x http://n.com:8080/p` (scheme `x http`!) |
| `'ht tp://a.com:80/p'` | `ht tp://n.com:80/p` (scheme `ht tp`, 80 kept) |
| `'http ://a.com:80/p'` | `http ://n.com:80/p` (scheme `http `, 80 kept) |

Derived rule for a reimplementer: a scheme is accepted by furl iff its first
character is an ASCII letter; almost anything else (space, TAB, `!`, `%`, `+`,
`.`, `-`, digits) is allowed after that. If the first character is C0/space the
authority is dropped entirely; if the first character is a non-letter,
non-C0/space, the entire string becomes the path.

## 8. IPv6 hosts

Default-port elision works identically for bracketed IPv6 literals; the port is
taken from after the closing `]`.

| `--a` (`--b n.com`) | output |
|---|---|
| `http://[::1]:80/p` | `http://n.com/p` (elided) |
| `http://[::1]:8080/p` | `http://n.com:8080/p` |
| `https://[2001:db8::1]:443/p` | `https://n.com/p` |
| `https://[::ffff:1.2.3.4]:443/p` | `https://n.com/p` |
| `https://[::ffff:1.2.3.4]:444/p` | `https://n.com:444/p` |
| `http://[::1]/p` | `http://n.com/p` |
| `http://[::1]:abc/p` | ValueError `Invalid port 'abc'.` |
| `http://[::1]:/p` | ValueError `Invalid port ''.` |
| `http://[::1]:0/p` | ValueError `Invalid port '0'.` |
| `http://[::1]:65535/p` | `http://n.com:65535/p` |
| `http://[::1]:65536/p` | ValueError `Invalid port '65536'.` |
| `http://u@[::1]:80/p` | `http://u@n.com/p` |
| `http://u:p@[::1]:8080/p` | `http://u:p@n.com:8080/p` |

`--b` may itself be a bracketed IPv6 literal, and elision still applies:
`http://a.com:80/p` + `[::1]` -> `http://[::1]/p`;
`http://a.com:8080/p` + `[::1]` -> `http://[::1]:8080/p`.

---

## 9. Userinfo does not disturb the port

The `@` split happens before the host/port split, so a colon inside the
userinfo is not a port delimiter.

| `--a` (`--b n.com`) | output |
|---|---|
| `http://user:pass@a.com:80/p` | `http://user:pass@n.com/p` |
| `http://user:pass@a.com:8080/p` | `http://user:pass@n.com:8080/p` |
| `http://user@a.com:80/p` | `http://user@n.com/p` |
| `http://user:pass@a.com/p` | `http://user:pass@n.com/p` |
| `http://:pass@a.com:80/p` | `http://:pass@n.com/p` |
| `http://a.com:80@b.com:8080/p` | `http://a.com:80@n.com:8080/p` (userinfo = `a.com:80`) |
| `http://user@:8080/p` | `http://user@n.com:8080/p` |
| `http://user@:80/p` | `http://user@n.com/p` |
| `ftp://u:p@a.com:21/x/y` | `ftp://u:p@n.com/x/y` |
| `ftp://u:p@a.com:22/x/y` | `ftp://u:p@n.com:22/x/y` |

An empty original host with a port is fine (the host is replaced by `--b`
anyway): `http://:80/p` -> `http://n.com/p`, `http://:8080/p` ->
`http://n.com:8080/p`, `//:8080/p` -> `//n.com:8080/p`.

---

## 10. `--b` interaction

`--b` sets **only** the host. It never changes, adds, or removes the port, and
default-port elision is evaluated after the host swap.

| `--a` | `--b` | output |
|---|---|---|
| `http://a.com:8080/p` | `other.example.org` | `http://other.example.org:8080/p` |
| `http://a.com:80/p` | `other.example.org` | `http://other.example.org/p` |
| `http://a.com:8080/p` | `ünïcode.com` | `http://xn--ncode-cta3g.com:8080/p` |
| `http://a.com:80/p` | `ünïcode.com` | `http://xn--ncode-cta3g.com/p` |
| `http://a.com:8080/p` | `127.0.0.1` | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/p` |
| `http://a.com:80/p` | `127.0.0.1` | `http://127.0.0.1/p` |
| `http://A.COM:80/p` | `N.COM` | `http://n.com/p` |
| `http://a.com:80/p` | `xn--ncode-cta3g.com` | `http://xn--ncode-cta3g.com/p` |

`--b ''` empties the host but keeps the port; elision still applies:

| `--a` | `--b` | output |
|---|---|---|
| `http://a.com:80/p` | `''` | `http:///p` |
| `https://a.com:443/p` | `''` | `https:///p` |
| `http://a.com:8080/p` | `''` | `http://:8080/p` |
| `zzz://a.com:80/p` | `''` | `zzz://:80/p` |
| `ws://a.com:80/p` | `''` | `ws:///p` |
| `ws://a.com:8080/p` | `''` | `ws://:8080/p` |
| `http://u@a.com:80/p` | `''` | `http://u@/p` |
| `http://u@a.com:8080/p` | `''` | `http://u@:8080/p` |
| `http://u:p@a.com:80/p` | `''` | `http://u:p@/p` |

`--b` containing a colon is rejected by host validation (so `--b` can never
supply a port): `--b 'n.com:8080'` ->
`ValueError: Invalid host 'n.com:8080'. Host strings must have at least one non-period character, can't contain any of '!@#$%^&'"*()+=:;/', and can't have adjacent periods.`
Same for `--b 'n.com:80'`, `--b '.'`, `--b '..'`, `--b '!bad!'`.

## 12. Things I could NOT determine

1. **Whether elision happens at parse time or render time.** Because `--b` only
   sets the host, the scheme can never change between parse and render, so
   "store `port=None` when it equals the default" and "compare at render time"
   are observationally identical here. Either implementation is byte-identical
   for this program.
2. **The `split('?')` branch of `is_valid_port`.** The traceback shows
   `is_valid_port` at `furl.py:133`; a port containing `?` or `#` is
   unreachable from URL parsing (both characters terminate the authority), so I
   could not test whether the validator strips a `?`-suffix. Irrelevant for
   this program.
3. **Whether the default-port table has entries for schemes I did not guess.**
   I probed ~150 scheme/port pairs across IANA well-known ports and popular
   non-standard schemes; the 45 hits in §2 are all I found. A scheme whose
   default port I guessed wrong would be misclassified as "no default" — the
   `nfs` (111 not 2049) and `rtspu` (5005 not 554) cases show this is a real
   hazard. Schemes in §2b were each probed with 1-3 candidate ports only.
4. **Exact scheme-validity predicate.** I established "first char must be an
   ASCII letter, later chars are permissive (space, TAB, `!`, `%`, `+`, `.`,
   `-`, digits all accepted)", but did not exhaustively map which later
   characters are rejected (e.g. `/`, `?`, `#` are structurally impossible to
   test in isolation). This matters only for §7c.
5. **NUL (`�`) at the start of the URL** could not be tested — it cannot
   be passed through `argv`. It is in the WHATWG C0 set, so it is *probably*
   handled like §7c, but this is unverified.
6. **Astral-plane digit port arithmetic beyond `𝟖𝟎`** — I confirmed
   `U+1D7D6..` maps correctly for one case but did not sweep all `Nd` blocks.

Witness: 'ventrilo://a.com:3784/p' -> 'ventrilo://n.com/p' but 'ventrilo://a.com:3785/p' -> 'ventrilo://n.com:3785/p'.

Render rule: emit ':'+String(port) after the host iff port is set AND port !== DEFAULT_PORTS[lowercase(scheme)]. The port is re-rendered as plain ASCII decimal from the parsed integer, so leading zeros and non-ASCII digits vanish: 'http://a.com:08080/p' -> 'http://n.com:8080/p'.

Schemes NOT in the table (port is never elided) include many that look like they should be: ftps(990), smtp(25), smtps(465), submission(587), imaps(993), pop3(110), pop3s(995), news(119), telnets(992), shttp(80), file, mailto, rtmp, rtmps, mysql, postgres, mongodb, amqp, coap, mqtt, sctp, stun, turn, sieve, whois, gemini, scp, svn+ssh, jabber, ldapi, socks, rdp. Two entries differ from the obvious IANA value: nfs default is 111 (NOT 2049) and rtspu default is 5005 (NOT 554). Witness: 'nfs://a.com:111/p' -> 'nfs://n.com/p' but 'nfs://a.com:2049/p' -> 'nfs://n.com:2049/p'; 'rtspu://a.com:5005/p' -> 'rtspu://n.com/p' but 'rtspu://a.com:554/p' -> 'rtspu://n.com:554/p'.
Scheme lookup uses the lowercased scheme. 'HTTP://a.com:80/p' -> 'http://n.com/p'; 'HtTp://a.com:80/p' -> 'http://n.com/p'; 'RTSPU://a.com:5005/p' -> 'rtspu://n.com/p'.
With no scheme there is no default port, so every port is preserved: '//a.com:80/p' -> '//n.com:80/p', '//a.com:443/p' -> '//n.com:443/p', '//:80/p' -> '//n.com:80/p'.

Port validity predicate: portStr must satisfy Python str.isdigit() AND int(portStr) must succeed AND 0 < value <= 65535. Leading zeros are legal and value-based: ':080' -> elided as 80, ':00001' -> ':1', ':0000065535' -> ':65535', ':0' / ':00' / ':0000' all raise, ':65535' ok, ':65536' raises.

Error form A (isdigit() false): stdout empty, exit 1, stderr last ValueError line is exactly "ValueError: Invalid port '<RAW>'." with the raw text echoed verbatim and a trailing period after the closing quote. Witnesses: ':abc' -> "Invalid port 'abc'."; ':80.' -> "Invalid port '80.'."; ':-1', ':+80', ':8.0', ':0x50', ':0b1010', ':1e2', ':8_0', ':%', ':%38%30', ':80%20', ': 80' (ASCII space), NBSP+'80', ZWSP+'80', ':½', ':⅓', ':Ⅷ'.

Error form B (isdigit() true but int() fails, i.e. Unicode Digit-but-not-Decimal): stderr last line is exactly "ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '<RAW>'" with NO trailing period. Witnesses: ':²' (superscript two), ':¹', ':³', ':⁴', ':₈', ':①' (circled one), ':⑧', ':⒏'.

Unicode DECIMAL digits (category Nd, any script, even mixed, including astral) are valid ports and are converted to their numeric value then compared against DEFAULT_PORTS: 'http://a.com:٨٠/p' (Arabic-Indic 80) -> 'http://n.com/p' (elided); 'http://a.com:٨٠٨٠/p' -> 'http://n.com:8080/p'; 'http://a.com:8๐/p' (ASCII 8 + Thai 0) -> 'http://n.com/p'; 'http://a.com:𝟖𝟎/p' -> 'http://n.com/p'.

An empty port after a colon is an error, not 'no port': 'http://a.com:/p', '//a.com:/p', 'zzz://a.com:/p', 'http://a.com:', 'http://a.com:?x=1', 'http://a.com:#f', 'http://[::1]:/p' all -> "ValueError: Invalid port ''."
The host/port split is rsplit(':', 1) on the post-userinfo part: 'http://a.com:80:90/p' -> "Invalid host 'a.com:80'." (port '90' was accepted) and 'http://a.com::80/p' -> "Invalid host 'a.com:'."

Port is validated BEFORE the host. 'http://a.com!:0/p' -> "Invalid port '0'." while 'http://a.com!:8080/p' -> "Invalid host 'a.com!'. ...". And --a is parsed before --b is validated: --a 'http://a.com:0/p' --b '!bad!' -> "Invalid port '0'."

IPv6: the port is taken after the closing bracket and elision works normally. 'http://[::1]:80/p' -> 'http://n.com/p'; 'http://[::1]:8080/p' -> 'http://n.com:8080/p'; 'https://[::ffff:1.2.3.4]:443/p' -> 'https://n.com/p'; 'http://[::1]:abc/p' -> "Invalid port 'abc'." A bracketed --b also works: 'http://a.com:80/p' + '[::1]' -> 'http://[::1]/p'.

Userinfo is split off at '@' before the port split, so colons inside it are inert: 'http://a.com:80@b.com:8080/p' -> 'http://a.com:80@n.com:8080/p'; 'http://user:pass@a.com:80/p' -> 'http://user:pass@n.com/p'; 'http://user@:80/p' -> 'http://user@n.com/p'.

--b only sets the host; it never touches the port, and elision is re-evaluated after the swap. 'http://a.com:8080/p' + 'unicode host ünïcode.com' -> 'http://xn--ncode-cta3g.com:8080/p'. --b '' keeps the port: 'http://a.com:8080/p' + '' -> 'http://:8080/p', while 'http://a.com:80/p' + '' -> 'http:///p' and 'http://u@a.com:80/p' + '' -> 'http://u@/p'. --b can never supply a port because a colon fails host validation: --b 'n.com:8080' -> "Invalid host 'n.com:8080'. ..."

TAB (\t), CR (\r) and LF (\n) are deleted from everything AFTER the scheme (netloc and path), so 'http://a.com:<TAB>80/p' -> 'http://n.com/p' (port==80, elided) and 'http://a.com:80/p<TAB>q' -> 'http://n.com/pq'. But they are PRESERVED inside the scheme, which then no longer matches the table: 'http<TAB>://a.com:80/p' -> 'http<TAB>://n.com:80/p' (80 kept).

If the URL's FIRST character is C0-control-or-space (0x00-0x20: space, \t, \n, \r, \v, \f, \x01, \x1f), the entire authority is discarded - scheme, userinfo, host AND port all vanish and NO port validation runs. ' http://a.com:8080/p' -> '//n.com/p'; ' http://a.com:0/p' -> '//n.com/p' with exit code 0 and no error; ' http://a.com!:8080/p' -> '//n.com/p' with no error. Contrast '\x7fhttp://a.com:8080/p' -> '//n.com/%7Fhttp://a.com:8080/p' (DEL is not in the C0 set).

A scheme is accepted iff its first character is an ASCII letter; later characters are very permissive (space, TAB, '!', '%', '+', '.', '-', digits all accepted) and such a scheme never matches the default-port table. 'ht tp://a.com:80/p' -> 'ht tp://n.com:80/p'; 'h%://a.com:80/p' -> 'h%://n.com:80/p'; but '1http://a.com:80/p' -> '//n.com/1http://a.com:80/p' (whole string becomes the path, so no port at all).

Port-looking text outside the authority is never a port: 'http://a.com/p:80' -> 'http://n.com/p:80'; 'http:a.com:80/p' -> 'http://n.com/a.com:80/p'; 'http:80/p' -> 'http://n.com/80/p'; 'a.com:80/p' -> 'a.com://n.com/80/p' (a.com is taken as the scheme).

Elision composes normally with empty path/query/fragment: 'http://a.com:80' -> 'http://n.com'; 'http://a.com:80/' -> 'http://n.com/'; 'http://a.com:80?x=1&y=2#f' -> 'http://n.com?x=1&y=2#f'; 'ldap://a.com:389/p?x=1#f' -> 'ldap://n.com/p?x=1#f'.

On any error: stdout is EMPTY, exit code is 1, and stderr carries a Python traceback whose final two lines are the ValueError line and "[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test2' due to unhandled exception!". The failing frame is furl/furl.py line 133 in is_valid_port (for form B) or line 1476 in port (for form A).
surprises: pop has default 110 but pop3 does NOT; nntp/nntps/snews have defaults but news does NOT; imap has one but imaps does NOT; ftp has one but ftps does NOT; sip/sips do but smtp/smtps do NOT. The table is not derivable from 'IANA scheme has a well-known port' - it must be hardcoded verbatim.
nfs's default is 111, not 2049. rtspu's default is 5005, not 554. Both would be gotten wrong by anyone consulting IANA for the 'obvious' value.

Non-ASCII Unicode DECIMAL digits are accepted as ports and numerically compared to the default table. 'http://a.com:٨٠/p' (Arabic-Indic eighty) silently becomes port 80 and is ELIDED, producing 'http://n.com/p'. Mixed scripts work too ('8' + Thai zero = 80).

There are TWO different ValueError messages for bad ports with different punctuation. Superscript/circled digits (², ①) pass str.isdigit() but fail int(), yielding "invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'" with NO trailing period, whereas everything else yields "Invalid port 'X'." WITH a trailing period.

Leading zeros are fully accepted and value-based: ':080' is port 80 and gets elided, ':00000000000000080' likewise, but ':00' and ':0000' raise because the value is 0. Reimplementers who regex on /^[1-9][0-9]*$/ will get all of these wrong.
An empty port ('http://a.com:/p') RAISES rather than being treated as absent. Even 'http://a.com:?x=1' and 'http://a.com:#f' raise.
The port is validated BEFORE the host, so a URL with both an invalid port and an invalid host reports the PORT error ('http://a.com!:0/p' -> Invalid port '0'.).

TAB/CR/LF are stripped from the authority (so 'http://a.com:<TAB>80/p' is port 80 and elides) but are KEPT in the scheme (so 'http<TAB>://a.com:80/p' has scheme 'http\t', misses the table, and keeps :80).

A single leading space (or any 0x00-0x20 char) makes the ENTIRE authority disappear - scheme, userinfo, host and port - and suppresses all port/host validation. ' http://a.com:0/p' exits 0 with output '//n.com/p' instead of raising Invalid port '0'.

Schemes with spaces are legal as long as the first char is a letter: 'ht tp://a.com:80/p' -> 'ht tp://n.com:80/p' and 'X http://a.com:8080/p' -> 'x http://n.com:8080/p'. But '1http://...' is not a scheme and the whole string becomes the path.
uncertainties: Whether elision happens at parse time (storing port=None when it equals the default) or at render time. Since --b cannot change the scheme, the two are observationally identical for this program.

The is_valid_port frame is furl.py:133 and furl likely does str(port).split('?')[0] first, but a port containing '?' or '#' is unreachable via URL parsing (both terminate the authority), so that branch could not be exercised.

Completeness of the 45-entry table depends on my guessing each scheme's default port correctly. ~150 scheme/port pairs were probed; a scheme whose real default I guessed wrong would be misfiled as 'no default'. The nfs(111 vs 2049) and rtspu(5005 vs 554) surprises show this is a real hazard. Schemes listed as having no default were each probed with only 1-3 candidate ports.

The exact scheme-validity predicate. I established 'first char must be an ASCII letter, later chars permissive', but did not exhaustively map which later characters are rejected (e.g. '/', '?', '#' are structurally untestable in isolation).
NUL (0x00) at the start of the URL could not be tested because it cannot be passed through argv. It is in the WHATWG C0 set so it probably behaves like the leading-space case, but this is unverified.

I confirmed one astral-plane Nd case (U+1D7D6 MATHEMATICAL BOLD DIGIT EIGHT) converts correctly, but did not sweep all Unicode Nd blocks; a JS implementation using /\p{Nd}/u plus per-block zero-offset arithmetic should match, but exotic blocks were not individually verified.

Whether the 11 duplicate lines in the corpus matter - they were genuine repeat runs and all produced identical output, so behavior is deterministic across runs, but I did not stress-test determinism broadly.
